claim: Lrp4 is the muscle receptor for neuronal Agrin.
source: Lrp4, the muscle receptor for neuronal Agrin, is expressed in the hippocampus and areas involved in cognition.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as established background information.

claim: Lrp4 is expressed in the hippocampus and areas involved in cognition.
source: Lrp4, the muscle receptor for neuronal Agrin, is expressed in the hippocampus and areas involved in cognition.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Lrp4−/− mice fail to form neuromuscular synapses and die at birth.
source: The function of Lrp4 in the brain, however, is unknown, as Lrp4−/− mice fail to form neuromuscular synapses and die at birth.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by prior literature cited in the introduction.

claim: Lrp4−/− mice rescued for Lrp4 expression selectively in muscle survive into adulthood.
source: Lrp4−/− mice, rescued for Lrp4 expression selectively in muscle, survive into adulthood and showed profound deficits in cognitive tasks that assess learning and memory.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in the results section with survival data.

claim: Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice showed profound deficits in cognitive tasks that assess learning and memory.
source: Lrp4−/− mice, rescued for Lrp4 expression selectively in muscle, survive into adulthood and showed profound deficits in cognitive tasks that assess learning and memory.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by behavioral data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: In the absence of Lrp4, the organization of the hippocampus appeared normal.
source: In the absence of Lrp4, the organization of the hippocampus appeared normal, but the frequency of spontaneous release events and spine density on primary apical dendrites were reduced.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 8A.

claim: The frequency of spontaneous release events is reduced in the absence of Lrp4.
source: In the absence of Lrp4, the organization of the hippocampus appeared normal, but the frequency of spontaneous release events and spine density on primary apical dendrites were reduced.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by mEPSC frequency data in Figure 5C,D.

claim: Spine density on primary apical dendrites is reduced in the absence of Lrp4.
source: In the absence of Lrp4, the organization of the hippocampus appeared normal, but the frequency of spontaneous release events and spine density on primary apical dendrites were reduced.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by spine density measurements in Figure 8B,C.

claim: CA3 input is unable to adequately depolarize CA1 neurons to induce long-term potentiation in the absence of Lrp4.
source: CA3 input was unable to adequately depolarize CA1 neurons to induce long-term potentiation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by LTP induction data in Figure 5.

claim: Mutations in genes encoding synaptic organizing complexes have been implicated in numerous and diverse neurological diseases, ranging from congenital myasthenia to autism spectrum disorders.
source: In humans, mutations in genes encoding synaptic organizing complexes have been implicated in numerous and diverse neurological diseases, ranging from congenital myasthenia to autism spectrum disorders (Sudhof, 2008; Burden et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Lrp4 plays a key role in the formation and maintenance of neuromuscular synapses.
source: Lrp4 plays a key role in the formation and maintenance of neuromuscular synapses, as a loss of Lrp4 leads to a failure to form neuromuscular synapses, and mutations in Lrp4 or auto-antibodies to Lrp4 cause congenital myasthenia and myasthenia gravis, respectively (Shen et al., 2013; Ohkawara et al., 2014; Tsivgoulis et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: A loss of Lrp4 leads to a failure to form neuromuscular synapses.
source: Lrp4 plays a key role in the formation and maintenance of neuromuscular synapses, as a loss of Lrp4 leads to a failure to form neuromuscular synapses, and mutations in Lrp4 or auto-antibodies to Lrp4 cause congenital myasthenia and myasthenia gravis, respectively (Shen et al., 2013; Ohkawara et al., 2014; Tsivgoulis et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Mutations in Lrp4 or auto-antibodies to Lrp4 cause congenital myasthenia and myasthenia gravis.
source: Lrp4 plays a key role in the formation and maintenance of neuromuscular synapses, as a loss of Lrp4 leads to a failure to form neuromuscular synapses, and mutations in Lrp4 or auto-antibodies to Lrp4 cause congenital myasthenia and myasthenia gravis, respectively (Shen et al., 2013; Ohkawara et al., 2014; Tsivgoulis et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Lrp4 functions bidirectionally at neuromuscular synapses.
source: Lrp4 functions bidirectionally at neuromuscular synapses, where it responds to neuronal Agrin, stimulating MuSK, a receptor tyrosine kinase that functions as a master regulator of synapse formation, and functions in a retrograde manner to stimulate differentiation of motor nerve terminals (Yumoto et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Lrp4 responds to neuronal Agrin, stimulating MuSK.
source: Lrp4 functions bidirectionally at neuromuscular synapses, where it responds to neuronal Agrin, stimulating MuSK, a receptor tyrosine kinase that functions as a master regulator of synapse formation, and functions in a retrograde manner to stimulate differentiation of motor nerve terminals (Yumoto et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: MuSK is a receptor tyrosine kinase that functions as a master regulator of synapse formation.
source: Lrp4 functions bidirectionally at neuromuscular synapses, where it responds to neuronal Agrin, stimulating MuSK, a receptor tyrosine kinase that functions as a master regulator of synapse formation, and functions in a retrograde manner to stimulate differentiation of motor nerve terminals (Yumoto et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Lrp4 functions in a retrograde manner to stimulate differentiation of motor nerve terminals.
source: Lrp4 functions bidirectionally at neuromuscular synapses, where it responds to neuronal Agrin, stimulating MuSK, a receptor tyrosine kinase that functions as a master regulator of synapse formation, and functions in a retrograde manner to stimulate differentiation of motor nerve terminals (Yumoto et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Lrp4 belongs to the low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR) family.
source: Lrp4 belongs to the low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR) family, an ancient group of endocytic type 1, single-pass transmembrane proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: LDLR family members are an ancient group of endocytic type 1, single-pass transmembrane proteins.
source: Lrp4 belongs to the low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR) family, an ancient group of endocytic type 1, single-pass transmembrane proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Lrp4 has multifunctional roles in tissues other than the nervous system, including bone homeostasis, limb patterning, kidney formation, and placode development.
source: Lrp4 has multifunctional roles in tissues other than the nervous system, including bone homeostasis, limb patterning, kidney formation, and placode development (Johnson et al., 2005; Weatherbee et al., 2006; Ohazama et al., 2008; Li et al., 2010; Ahn et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Lrp4 is expressed in the central nervous system (CNS) as well as in the peripheral nervous system.
source: Lrp4 is expressed in the central nervous system (CNS) as well as in the peripheral nervous system (Visel et al., 2004; Tian et al., 2006; Weatherbee et al., 2006; Lein et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Within the CNS, Lrp4 is expressed prominently in the hippocampus, olfactory bulb, cerebellum, and neocortex.
source: Within the CNS, Lrp4 is expressed prominently in the hippocampus, olfactory bulb, cerebellum, and neocortex and present in postsynaptic membranes (Tian et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Lrp4 is present in postsynaptic membranes in the CNS.
source: Within the CNS, Lrp4 is expressed prominently in the hippocampus, olfactory bulb, cerebellum, and neocortex and present in postsynaptic membranes (Tian et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Lrp4 mutant mice die at birth from neuromuscular and respiratory failure, before synapse formation in the CNS ensues.
source: The role of Lrp4 in the CNS is not understood, as Lrp4 mutant mice die at birth from neuromuscular and respiratory failure, before synapse formation in the CNS ensues (De Felipe et al., 1997; Tian et al., 2006; Weatherbee et al., 2006; Kim et al., 2008; Yumoto et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Muscle-selective expression of Lrp4 (Lrp4m) rescued the neuromuscular deficits of Lrp4 mutant mice, allowing the mice to survive as adults.
source: Previously, we generated mice that lack Lrp4 in all tissues except skeletal muscle and found that muscle-selective expression of Lrp4 (Lrp4m) rescued the neuromuscular deficits of Lrp4 mutant mice, allowing the mice to survive as adults (Gomez and Burden, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation to prior work.

claim: Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice retained the fused digit and appendage defects found in Lrp4 mutant mice.
source: Newborn mice, which lack Lrp4 in all tissues except skeletal muscle (Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m), retained the fused digit and appendage defects found in Lrp4 mutant mice.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 1A inset.

claim: By three weeks after birth the growth rate of Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice began to slow.
source: By three weeks after birth the growth rate of Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice began to slow and by 6 weeks the mice were modestly runted (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 1B.

claim: By 6 weeks the Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice were modestly runted.
source: By three weeks after birth the growth rate of Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice began to slow and by 6 weeks the mice were modestly runted (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 1B.

claim: The body mass of six-week old Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice is reduced by 16%.
source: The body mass of six-week old Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice is reduced by 16% (wild-type, 21.4 ± 0.8 g, n = 10; Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m, 18.0 ± 0.5 g, n = 5).
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1B with specific measurements.

claim: Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice were fertile and lived a normal lifespan.
source: Nonetheless, Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice were fertile and lived a normal lifespan, indicating that Lrp4 is not required in tissues other than muscle for postnatal survival.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: Lrp4 is not required in tissues other than muscle for postnatal survival.
source: Nonetheless, Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice were fertile and lived a normal lifespan, indicating that Lrp4 is not required in tissues other than muscle for postnatal survival.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the survival data.

claim: The macroscopic morphology of the brain from adult Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice appeared normal.
source: The macroscopic morphology of the brain from adult Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice appeared normal, although brain size, like body mass, was modestly reduced (Figure 1C,D).

claim: Brain size in Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice was modestly reduced.
source: The macroscopic morphology of the brain from adult Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice appeared normal, although brain size, like body mass, was modestly reduced (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The size of the adult brain is reduced by 11% in Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice.
source: The size of the adult brain is reduced by 11% in Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice (wild-type, 0.45 ± 0.005 g, n = 17; Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m, 0.4 ± 0.008 g, n = 15).
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1D with specific measurements.

claim: The locomotor activity of Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice in an open field test was normal as measured by distance traveled, mean velocity, and maximum velocity.
source: The locomotor activity of Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice in an open field test was normal as measured by distance traveled (E), mean velocity (F), and maximum velocity (G) (wild-type, n = 17; Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m, n = 15).
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1E-G and shown in the data.

claim: Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice do not have obvious motor or skeletal defects.
source: When placed in the open-field arena, Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice traveled as far and fast as control animals (Figure 1E–G), indicating that Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice do not have obvious motor or skeletal defects.

claim: Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice showed reduced exploratory behavior.
source: Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice showed reduced exploratory behavior (wild-type, 22.3 ± 2.2%, n = 29; Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m, 14.9 ± 1.2%, n = 25).

claim: Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice avoided the center of the arena in the open field test.
source: The heat map in Figure 1I shows that control mice roamed throughout the open-field, whereas Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice avoided the center of the arena (Figure 1H,I).

claim: When suspended by the tail, Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice display a stereotyped limb clasping behavior.
source: Additionally, when suspended by the tail, Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice display a stereotyped limb clasping behavior, similar to other mouse models of neurological disorders, including Rett Syndrome (Figure 2) (Guy et al., 2001).

claim: Limb clasping behavior is similar to other mouse models of neurological disorders, including Rett Syndrome.
source: Additionally, when suspended by the tail, Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice display a stereotyped limb clasping behavior, similar to other mouse models of neurological disorders, including Rett Syndrome (Figure 2) (Guy et al., 2001).

claim: During training in fear conditioning, both control and Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice responded similarly to the tone and foot shock.
source: During training, both control and Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice responded similarly to the tone and foot shock (Figure 3A), demonstrating that these sensory systems remained intact in the rescued mice.

claim: Sensory systems remained intact in Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice.
source: During training, both control and Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice responded similarly to the tone and foot shock (Figure 3A), demonstrating that these sensory systems remained intact in the rescued mice.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the fear conditioning data.

claim: Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice spent much less time freezing in response to the tone alone in fear conditioning.
source: As expected, wild-type mice froze in response to the tone alone. In contrast, Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice spent much less time freezing, suggesting impaired learning or memory for the tone–shock pairing (Figure 3A).

claim: Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice have impaired learning or memory for the tone–shock pairing.
source: As expected, wild-type mice froze in response to the tone alone. In contrast, Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice spent much less time freezing, suggesting impaired learning or memory for the tone–shock pairing (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the fear conditioning data.

claim: Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice have an impaired association of the dark chamber with the foot shock in passive avoidance.
source: Control mice were slow to enter the dark chamber after training, whereas Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice entered the dark chamber with a shorter latency than control mice, indicating an impaired association of the dark chamber with the foot shock (Figure 3B).

Although the latency for Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice also decreased during this training period, they consistently took longer to find the platform than control mice (Figures 3C and 4B).

claim: Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice crossed the former platform location with similar frequency to control mice in the probe trial.

source: These findings indicate that while the rescued mice had difficulty learning the position of the hidden platform; however, with repeated training, they were able to learn the position and eventually behave in a manner similar to control mice.

claim: Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice spent less time than control mice in the new target region during reversal training.
source: Control mice rapidly learned the new location of the platform, whereas Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice showed a significant impairment (Figures 3C and 4D) and spent less time than control mice in the new target region (Figure 3G).

claim: Control and Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice had comparable swimming velocities in the Morris water maze.

claim: The impaired performance of Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice in the Morris water maze was not due to compromised visual acuity, swimming ability, or motivation to escape the water.
source: Control and Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice were similarly able to locate a visible platform and had comparable swimming velocities, indicating that the impaired performance of Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice was not due to compromised visual acuity, swimming ability, or motivation to escape the water (Figure 3C,D, 4E).

claim: Paired-pulse facilitation was similar in control and Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice.
source: Paired-pulse facilitation was similar in control and Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice, indicating that Lrp4 is not essential for this form of evoked transmitter release and short-term plasticity (Figure 5B).

claim: Lrp4 is not essential for paired-pulse facilitation and short-term plasticity.
source: Paired-pulse facilitation was similar in control and Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice, indicating that Lrp4 is not essential for this form of evoked transmitter release and short-term plasticity (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the paired-pulse facilitation data.

claim: mEPSC frequency was reduced twofold in Lrp4 mutant neurons.
source: Next, we examined basal activity by measuring spontaneous miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSC) in CA1 neurons. mEPSC frequency was reduced twofold in Lrp4 mutant neurons (Figure 5C,D), although the mEPSC amplitude was normal (Figure 5C,E,F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: mEPSC amplitude was normal in Lrp4 mutant neurons.
source: Next, we examined basal activity by measuring spontaneous miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSC) in CA1 neurons. mEPSC frequency was reduced twofold in Lrp4 mutant neurons (Figure 5C,D), although the mEPSC amplitude was normal (Figure 5C,E,F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 5C,E,F.

claim: The lower mEPSC frequency could be due to a reduced probability of vesicle fusion or a reduction in the number of synapses on CA1 neurons.
source: The lower mEPSC frequency could be due to a reduced probability of vesicle fusion or a reduction in the number of synapses on CA1 neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as speculation about the mechanism.

claim: TBS induced robust LTP from wild-type CA1 neurons.
source: TBS induced robust LTP from wild-type CA1 neurons (Figure 5G,L,N), whereas TBS failed to induce LTP in Lrp4−/− CA1 neurons (Figure 5H,M,N).

claim: TBS failed to induce LTP in Lrp4−/− CA1 neurons.
source: TBS induced robust LTP from wild-type CA1 neurons (Figure 5G,L,N), whereas TBS failed to induce LTP in Lrp4−/− CA1 neurons (Figure 5H,M,N).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 5H,M,N.

claim: During the induction procedure the amplitudes of TBS-evoked EPSCs were reduced in Lrp4−/− CA1 neurons compared to wild-type.
source: During the induction procedure the amplitudes of TBS-evoked EPSCs were reduced in Lrp4−/− CA1 neurons compared to wild-type (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Lrp4 is critical for a form of synaptic plasticity that has been linked to learning and memory.
source: This dramatic loss of LTP demonstrates that Lrp4 is critical for a form of synaptic plasticity that has been linked to learning and memory.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the LTP data.

claim: The smaller EPSCs during TBS in Lrp4−/− CA1 neurons prevented LTP induction in these cells.
source: We hypothesized that the smaller EPSCs during TBS in Lrp4−/− CA1 neurons prevented LTP induction in these cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a hypothesis.

claim: Induction of LTP in CA1 neurons requires that SC-released glutamate binds to AMPA receptors to depolarize postsynaptic neurons to a level sufficient to release the Mg2+-block of NMDA receptors and drive Ca2+ influx into postsynaptic compartments.
source: Induction of LTP in CA1 neurons requires that SC-released glutamate binds to AMPA receptors to depolarize postsynaptic neurons to a level sufficient to release the Mg2+-block of NMDA receptors and drive Ca2+ influx into postsynaptic compartments (Nowak et al., 1984; Collingridge et al., 1988).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: Brief depolarization of CA1 neurons to 0 mV during TBS was sufficient to restore normal TBS-induced LTP in Lrp4−/− neurons.

evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 5J,K,M,N.

claim: Expression of LTP in Lrp4−/− CA1 neurons is intact as long as CA1 neurons are adequately depolarized during TBS.
source: Importantly, these data show that expression of LTP in Lrp4−/− CA1 neurons is intact as long as CA1 neurons are adequately depolarized during TBS.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the depolarization rescue data.

claim: CA3 SCs appear unable to depolarize CA1 neurons to a level required to recruit NMDA receptors.
source: Thus, CA3 SCs appear unable to depolarize CA1 neurons to a level required to recruit NMDA receptors.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the LTP rescue data.

claim: AMPA and NMDA receptors are expressed at normal levels in synaptosomes isolated from Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m hippocampus.

evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: Inhibition was modestly reduced at low stimulation intensities in Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice.
source: Contrary to this notion, we found that inhibition was modestly reduced at low stimulation intensities and unchanged at higher stimulation intensities in Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Inhibition was unchanged at higher stimulation intensities in Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice.
source: Contrary to this notion, we found that inhibition was modestly reduced at low stimulation intensities and unchanged at higher stimulation intensities in Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 7G.

claim: The E/I ratio at CA1 synapses was diminished in Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice.
source: Because excitation was reduced while inhibition remained largely unaffected (Figures 5,7), the E/I ratio at CA1 synapses was diminished (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 7H.

claim: Enhanced inhibition is not responsible for the failure to elicit LTP in Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice.
source: Together, these data are inconsistent with the idea that enhanced inhibition is responsible for a failure to elicit LTP and instead favor the idea that a failure of presynaptic input to adequately depolarize CA1 neurons underlies the LTP deficit.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the inhibition data.

claim: A failure of presynaptic input to adequately depolarize CA1 neurons underlies the LTP deficit in Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice.
source: Together, these data are inconsistent with the idea that enhanced inhibition is responsible for a failure to elicit LTP and instead favor the idea that a failure of presynaptic input to adequately depolarize CA1 neurons underlies the LTP deficit.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the combined data.

claim: The distribution of DAPI-stained nuclei and NeuN were comparable in slices from wild-type and Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice.
source: The distribution of DAPI-stained nuclei and NeuN, a neuronal transcription factor, were comparable in slices from wild-type and Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The distributions of the presynaptic marker Synapsin and the excitatory postsynaptic marker PSD95 were similar in sections from wild-type and rescued mice.
source: Additionally, the distributions of the presynaptic marker Synapsin and the excitatory postsynaptic marker PSD95 were similar in sections from wild-type and rescued mice (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The defects in synaptic transmission and plasticity in Lrp4−/−; Lrp4m mice were not accompanied by a gross morphological disorganization of the hippocampus.
